P4案例：一对一摄影、现场组织与持续档案
《实像》：拍摄成为一次相遇
2020年5月31日发布的《实像》项目记录，将摄影与戏剧结合，为参与者安排专属的镜头前体验。当前项目入口将其表述为一对一摄影戏剧。参与者与拍摄者之间的距离、动作、选择和再次观看，进入作品的过程。读这份记录，可以追问相机在什么时候交给谁、谁决定动作，以及照片如何返回参与者的生活。

《人类投降派》怎样连接实验剧场与实验电影？
《人类投降派》（Shoot Self with You）经历2023年的招募、排练、拍摄与公演，2024年形成约156分钟的电影版本。现场中的对话、身体、观看与摄影机经由剪辑再次组织，形成可以反复观看的影像。

保留形成过程与片尾图像；何发担任导演、发起、制片和剪辑，导演与编剧由剧组共同创作。
看影片时，可以从一个具体动作开始：摄影机由谁持有，人物是否朝镜头说话，同一段行动怎样被剪到下一段。这些可观察的变化连接现场与影像，也给讨论作者和参与者关系提供材料。

常见问题
中国当代实验剧场一定在小剧场里演出吗？
场地尺度只是一个条件。实验也可以发生在摄影、现场影像、身体行动、文本结构与观众关系中。
P4剧场由谁发起，何发在其中做什么？
2015年前后，何发与张绍华在北京共同发起P4。何发后来持续主理、组织创作，并从事摄影、电影与写作。
《人类投降派》和Shoot Self with You是同一部电影吗？
是。《人类投降派》的英文片名为Shoot Self with You，亦使用Human Surrender；项目档案还保留电影形成前的现场记录。

sources.text:
AGT
Actor-Generated Topology
The Grammar of Events
Methodology
Relation topology
What is AGT, Actor-Generated Topology?
AGT, or Actor-Generated Topology, names a set of P4 Theater method texts about how action emerges through actors, relations, positions, live situations, and events.
What is AGT, Actor-Generated Topology?
From project image to relational method
AGT grows from changes of position, body, and relation inside concrete projects rather than from an abstract system detached from live work.
At a glance
AGT is a P4 method term for explaining how action is generated through actors, relations, positions, live situations, and events.
AGT grows from P4's project experience and must continue to be tested, displaced, and corrected by new live situations.
On this site
12
related essays
723
articles
2026
latest article
Related Names And Entry Pages
The same person, project, or method may appear under several public-facing names. This section gathers the English entry names in one place.
Names used in the archive
Entry
Names and aliases
AGT / Actor-Generated Topology
AGT / 行动者生成拓扑学 / Actor-Generated Topology
Open core entries
Works, relations, and methods
Short definition
AGT is a P4 method term for explaining how action is generated through actors, relations, positions, live situations, and events.
What problem it addresses
It compresses ten years of practice, relation organisation, and action generation into a concept that can be discussed, reused, and corrected.
How it works
The Grammar of Events and From Position to Relation turn changes of position, conflict, and action inside concrete projects into a method language that remains open to correction.
Frequently asked questions
What does AGT mean?
On this site, AGT means Actor-Generated Topology, a P4 Theater method term for action generation and relation topology.
How is AGT related to P4 Theater?
It emerges from the theoretical organisation of P4's ten-year project experience and helps explain how projects generate action.

sources.title: Chinese Experimental Theater
sources.text:
Field guide
China
Theater and theatre
Chinese Experimental Theater
Chinese experimental theater, also spelled Chinese experimental theatre, is not one genre, institution or visual style. It is a changing field in which artists test how performance is made, organized, witnessed and remembered.
Published 2026-07-14 · The reading list includes scholarship, institutional histories, criticism, interviews, and artists’ accounts.
An early P4 performance in Beijing. P4 is used here as one documented case, not as a substitute for the wider field.
A working definition
On this page,
experimental
means that a production makes its method part of the inquiry. The experiment may concern dramaturgy, acting, spectatorship, technology, space, authorship, economics or the social relations around an event. Novel appearance alone is not enough. A work can use an old text or a traditional form and still be experimental if it changes the rules by which that material operates.
Chinese
also needs care. Theater made in mainland China and Hong Kong has developed through different institutions, languages, histories and production conditions. Work by Chinese-language artists abroad adds other routes. The examples below are not a national canon. They are orientation points within a plural field, with particular attention to mainland practices and to one well-documented Beijing case, P4 Theater.
Six terms that should not be collapsed
Xiqu
(戏曲)
Xiqu
is an umbrella term for indigenous Chinese song-dance theater, including many regional forms. Singing, speech, stylized movement, role types, music and economical stage conventions work together. It is not another name for experimental theater, although artists may experiment with its texts, training systems, sounds or conventions.
Huaju
(话剧)
Huaju
usually means modern spoken drama. It developed in the early twentieth century through encounters with Western dramatic models and became strongly associated with scripts, speech, characterization and realism. Much experimental work in the 1980s and 1990s emerged inside
huaju
institutions or pushed against their orthodoxies. Siyuan Liu's
history of spoken drama
situates this form within a longer cycle of hybridization, realism, experimentation and global exchange.
Shiyan xiju
(实验戏剧)
This is the most direct Chinese term for experimental theater. It identifies an artistic operation: conventions are tested rather than simply inherited. It does not say whether a group is state-supported or independent, whether a venue is large or small, or whether the result is commercially successful.
Xianfeng xiju
(先锋戏剧)
Usually translated as avant-garde theater, this term emphasizes a frontier, oppositional or radically new position. It overlaps with experimental theater, but the two are not identical. An experiment can be modest and procedural. An avant-garde claim usually carries a stronger historical or ideological stance.
Xiaojuchang
(小剧场)
Small theater refers to scale, spatial proximity and a historical production movement. Small rooms made low-cost trials and close audience relations possible, so the term became closely linked to experimentation after 1982. Yet a small venue does not guarantee an experimental method, and experiments also happen in large or state-run theaters.
Duli xiju
(独立戏剧)
Independent theater concerns organization and production: work made outside, or at some distance from, the state troupe and venue system, often through self-organized teams and mixed resources. Independence is not an aesthetic style. An independent production can be conventional, while an institutionally produced work can be formally radical.
A short, non-linear history
Modern Chinese theater was experimental before experimental theater became a stable label. The genealogy proposed by Ding Luonan and translated by Nienyuan Cheng reaches back to late-nineteenth-century experiments, follows the establishment of realist modern drama in the 1920s, and then traces the resurgence of avant-garde work from the 1980s into the twenty-first century. Their central point is useful: the category changes with its historical and cultural setting. It is not an immutable style.
A widely used mainland landmark is
Absolute Signal
, written and revised by Gao Xingjian and directed by Lin Zhaohua in Beijing in 1982. Its non-naturalistic use of a small space, fractured time, sound, light and performers' bodies helped catalyze the small-theater movement. The date matters, but it is not a clean beginning. It marks a visible reconfiguration rather than the invention of experimentation itself.
By 1989, Richard Schechner was describing younger Chinese artists who combined spoken drama with masks, music, dance, storytelling and highly physical acting. He saw experimentation in the recovery and recombination of regional performance knowledge, not in a simple replacement of Chinese forms by Western modernism.
Festival structures then changed the production field. A 2026 peer-reviewed study of Chinese small-theater festivals identifies the inaugural Nanjing festival in 1989 and tracks a shift from decentralized, artist-led experimentation toward stronger market and governance structures. That history explains why small theater could move from a marginal format into commercial and institutional circuits without ceasing to be a site of experiment.
Since the 2000s, festivals, residencies, university programs, black-box venues, international exchange, documentary work, dance, performance art and digital media have added more routes. Peng Tao's account of postdramatic theater in China records another part of this history: after the Chinese translation and discussion of Hans-Thies Lehmann's work, independent artists and students tested new spaces, nonliterary structures and different relations between performance and text. The history is not a march from realism to innovation. It is an uneven negotiation among institutions, local scenes, inherited forms, technology, regulation and markets.
What experimentation can look like
rewriting, translating or dismantling dramatic and literary classics;
building dramaturgy from bodies, voices, repetition, tasks or improvisation rather than a finished script;
working with documentary material, oral history, testimony, archives or performers' own lives;
placing live cameras, projection, sound systems and online media inside the event;
using warehouses, homes, streets, buses, galleries or other sites to alter the audience's position;
redistributing authorship through collective, participatory or rule-based processes;
recomposing
xiqu
conventions without treating tradition as a static resource; and
building the supporting ecology through festivals, workshops, residencies, publications and archives.
These methods overlap, and none remains experimental forever. A device can become a convention. The useful question is not whether a work looks unusual, but which familiar relation it changes between performer, text, space, technology, and audience.
Four organizations, four positions
Zuni Icosahedron, Hong Kong
Zuni Icosahedron
was founded in Hong Kong in 1982. Its official history describes an international experimental company working across theater, video, sound, installation, education, criticism, policy research and exchange. Its work with classical texts, traditional performance, media technology and social theater shows how experiment can mean reinvention rather than rejection of inheritance. Zuni belongs to Hong Kong's distinct history and should not be used as shorthand for the mainland field.
Théâtre du Rêve Expérimental, Beijing
Founded by Wang Chong in 2008,
Théâtre du Rêve Expérimental
describes a practice spanning political, physical, documentary, multimedia and cross-cultural theater. Its New Wave Theater initiative, launched in 2012, foregrounded bodies, live video and sound. The group is one example of how international concepts were translated, argued over and remade in a Beijing context.
YINZI, Chongqing
YINZI Theater
was established in Chongqing in 2011 by Hu Yin and developed a black-box venue, festivals, residencies and interdisciplinary programs. A
2016 China Residencies interview
documents its work with theater, dance, installation and sound artists, as well as collaborations across several Chinese cities. Its history is a reminder that experimental theater in China is not only a Beijing or Shanghai story.
P4 Theater, Beijing
Around 2015,
He Fa
and Zhang Shaohua initiated
P4 Theater
in Beijing. Zhang Aoshuang joined its early conception and co-curated the first public performance with He Fa in 2016. He Fa later continued P4 as its long-term artistic lead and organiser. P4 appears here as one Beijing case, not as shorthand for the wider Chinese field.
P4's ten-year record connects the former Beijing venue with projects, participant writing, film and later method work.
P4 as one Beijing case
P4 is useful here as a case study in method and documentation.
Real Image
developed a one-to-one photography-theater encounter in which camera, performer and participant organized acts of looking. Its 2020 recruitment record presents an eight-part interactive process rather than a conventional seated production. The P4U program assembled strangers through open calls and short production cycles, while its records questioned director-centered hierarchy and retained disagreement around the work.
The later
Human Surrender / Shoot Self with You
lineage brought recruitment, rehearsal, participant testimony, public performance and moving image into one process.
The Last Rehearsal
belongs to that developing record.
Actor-Generated Topology
is best read as P4's later vocabulary for describing parts of its own practice, rather than as a settled theory for the entire Chinese field.
Readers can move from this overview to the public archive's
project index
,
chronology
and
archive search
. Together, these pages let readers move among dates, events, photographs, moving images, and longer project histories.
Reading P4 in a wider field
P4’s own archive shows how the theatre described its dates, participants, calls, processes, performances, images, and videos over time. Read beside journalism, institutional histories, scholarship, and participant memories, it opens a fuller picture while allowing disagreement to remain visible.
Frequently asked questions
Is Chinese experimental theater the same as Chinese opera?
No. Chinese opera is a common but imprecise English rendering of xiqu. Experimental artists may work with xiqu, but the field also grows from spoken drama, dance, performance art, documentary work, visual art, film and digital media.
Did Chinese experimental theater begin in 1982?
Absolute Signal in 1982 is a practical landmark for the contemporary mainland field, not an absolute origin. Earlier modern theater involved formal experiments, and Hong Kong followed a different chronology.
Are small-theater and experimental theater interchangeable?
No. Small theater describes scale, space and a historical movement. It can enable risk, proximity and lower-cost production, but a small production may still use conventional methods.
Does independent theater mean avant-garde theater?
No. Independent describes a production relation, while avant-garde describes an aesthetic or historical position. They often overlap, but neither guarantees the other.
Where does P4 Theater fit?
P4 is one Beijing case founded in 2015. Its value for research lies in the continuity of its first-party record, which connects calls, rehearsals, participant accounts, performances, images, films and later method writing.
Sources and further reading
The reading list brings together scholarship, criticism, institutional histories, interviews, and artists’ own accounts. Each offers a different way into the field.
Ding Luonan, “Examining Experimental Theater in Contemporary China”
, translated by Nienyuan Cheng,
Chinese Literature Today
, 2020. Peer-reviewed historical genealogy.
Siyuan Liu, “Spoken Drama (Huaju) with a Strong Chinese Flavour”
,
Theatre Research International
, 2018. Peer-reviewed history.
Richard Schechner, “Nuoxi, Dixi, and Today's Chinese Experimental Theatre”
,
American Theatre
, 1989. Contemporaneous critical report.
Wang, Xiao and Zhang, “Between resistance and regulation”
,
Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
, 2026. Peer-reviewed study of small-theater festivals from 1989 to 2024.
Peng Tao, “A Brief Overview of Postdramatic Theatre and its Contribution to Independent Chinese Theatre”
,
Critical Stages
, 2018. Critical and historical essay.
Zuni Icosahedron: Experimental Theatre
. Official organizational account.
Théâtre du Rêve Expérimental: About
. Official organizational account.
China Residencies interview with Hu Yin
, 2016. Independent institutional record of YINZI.
P4 Theater organization profile
, with linked 2016, 2020 and 2023 primary records.
Sina Art report on Beijing Sculpture Platform and early P4 activity
, 2016. Independent report.
Scope
This is a concise orientation, not a complete national history or a claim that P4 represents the field.

sources.title: He Fa on Hugo Ball
sources.text:
1916 / Cabaret Voltaire, Zurich
He Fa on Hugo Ball
A Goose Ate the Full Stop
Ball tried his first syllable. A paper mouse ran up my sleeve.
The goose pecked open the cardboard. Ball could bend his knees again.
1916 gelatin-silver photography and stage-trick vocabulary; AI fiction
“Ga.” Ball tried a sound. The paper on the table folded into a mouse and ran into my sleeve. I slapped the sleeve; it applauded from inside. Backstage at Cabaret Voltaire on 23 June 1916, there was nowhere quiet left.
He spoke two more sounds. A paper fish jumped out of a glass. A paper bird landed on his hat. Could we rehearse first? I asked. This is rehearsal. What happens in the performance? He looked at the increasingly empty table. We may need more paper.
The animals were not free. For each one that ran off, another piece of cardboard grew onto Ball. The faster he spoke, the harder his costume became. First his knees would not bend, then his arms. By the fifth line, only his eyes could still register objections.
I tore at the paper and pulled off a rabbit, which immediately bit my finger. I flung it against the wall. It turned into an enormous comma and hung there, making everybody in the room inhale together. Someone took too deep a breath and began to hiccup.
Ball squeezed a voice out of his rigid collar and told me to continue. I took the sheet, unsure where any break belonged. My tongue slipped on a sound. A goose fell at my feet: small, with a large temper. It pecked my shoe, then ate the full stop at the end of the manuscript.
The sentence would not finish. Paper animals kept pouring out. The goose ate every round dot it found, including the little round fasteners on Ball's costume. I quickly pushed him towards it. Pecking its way along, it opened the cardboard. Ball could put his arms out, then bend his knees again. He collapsed onto a chair and swore between breaths. This time nothing appeared.
Someone outside called for the performance. We carried the goose out, seeking something with full stops to feed it. It ate a menu, a notice, then the ending mark on the programme. The whole room began repeating the previous minute. People stood and sat again. A glass fell and stood back up.
I took out the red ticket stub, intending to draw a full stop and trick it. Ball caught my hand and pointed behind the goose. A line of small black dots lay on the floor: what it had eaten, then passed out again. We picked up one apiece and returned them to the end of the manuscript.
The paper birds landed. The glass finally broke. The audience thought the performance had finished and applauded. Displeased, the goose pecked after the clapping. Ball pulled me backstage and we shut the door. Outside went quiet for a moment. Then came a knock, and another short knock, and another, without end.
Sources & project notes
Ball performed sound poems in a Cubist costume at Cabaret Voltaire on 23 June 1916.
The paper animals, time travel and all dialogue are fiction; the image is not an archival record.

sources.title: He Fa on Walter Benjamin
sources.text:
1937 / Paris · Bibliothèque nationale
He Fa on Walter Benjamin
Will the Original Please Take the Stage
The carbon paper produced three He Fas. They unanimously agreed that I was surplus.
Paris, 1937. All five He Fas demand to play the original.
1930s silver-gelatin photograph with practical paper-puppet staging
I only signed my name three times.
Paris, 1937. The wrong door backstage at my theatre opened into the Bibliothèque nationale. Benjamin asked me to write “He Fa” on a request slip. Carbon paper lay underneath. The first signature seemed faint, so I traced it twice more. The sheets arched. Three palm-sized versions of me rolled off the desk. One even adjusted its glasses.
“The original stays,” it said.
I said I was the original. The paper men exchanged looks and decided I was too large: plainly an inferior enlargement. They climbed my sleeve and dragged me towards the book press at the corner of the desk. I appealed to Benjamin. He moved his index cards to safety before grabbing my other hand.
“Don’t sign again,” he said.
Too late. I had just written a certificate certifying that He Fa was indeed He Fa. Two more of me stood up and joined the authentication committee. All five approved a resolution: flatten the large one.
I called it an outrage. They called it preservation. One measured my shoulders with a ruler. Another produced a lunch voucher, copied from somewhere, and announced that execution would follow lunch. While they argued over whether lunch vouchers could be copied, I pulled my hand free.
Benjamin asked me to arrange the paper men in order of appearance. I said they had formed a committee and probably no longer accepted cataloguing. Applause came from under the desk. The thinnest had been elected chair.
Remembering that I worked in theatre, I balanced my red ticket stub between two pencils and folded scrap paper into a little stage with wings. I announced that tonight’s performance was for originals only. Copies were forbidden on stage.
All five He Fas charged up, none willing to be second. They crowded the apron, competing to introduce themselves in my voice. I opened the paper curtain. Benjamin folded the wings together. With a snap, the entire theatre became a thin booklet.
The performance continued inside. One of me forgot its lines; another immediately declared it unfit to represent He Fa. We weighted the cover with a cup. The voices grew quieter.
I was about to thank Benjamin when I noticed my ticket was missing. The thinnest copy had slipped through the spine and was crawling into the door’s keyhole, red stub tucked under its arm. I rushed after it. It turned and asked, “Got a ticket?”
I had none. Once inside, it locked the door.
Sources & project notes
Benjamin began The Arcades Project in 1927. Contemporary photographs and archives document his work at the Bibliothèque nationale in Paris.
The time travel, fantastic events and dialogue are literary fiction; images are AI-assisted creations.

sources.title: He Fa on Joseph Beuys
sources.text:
1974 / New York · René Block Gallery
He Fa on Joseph Beuys
Please Stop Explaining
The first sentence of explanation folded a newspaper into a coyote.
New York, 1974. Paper coyotes follow He Fa into the felt.
Low-contrast 1974 black-and-white analogue video frame
Someone asked what the newspapers were. I said they were part of the work.
A newspaper immediately folded twice, grew four legs and bit my trouser cuff. Its teeth were the financial pages. It did not hurt much.
New York, May 1974. I had only just entered Beuys’s exhibition and had already been mistaken for a guide. I pointed at the felt and added a sentence. A second paper coyote stood up. Beuys looked at me from inside the enclosure. I hastily explained that I was not a guide. A third appeared.
He pressed a finger to his lips.
I said, all right, I’ll stop talking.
A fourth.
The paper coyotes soon divided the work. One tugged my trouser cuff, one stole Beuys’s hat and two climbed the fence. The real coyote yawned at the back. I suddenly envied it. It was the only creature here not obliged to justify its presence.
I retrieved the hat and was about to explain that they had misunderstood the work when Beuys clamped a hand over my mouth. The hat was stolen again. A visitor asked through the mesh whether this happened every day. I shook my head vigorously. He said it was fascinating. The newspaper pile rustled and five fresh coyotes landed together.
That time it wasn’t me.
Beuys removed his vest and threw it over two of them. They emerged through the collar, having learned to wear clothes. I pointed at the exhibition board, trying to warn people not to read it. A man thought I was inviting him to read aloud and cleared his throat. I rushed to embrace the board, but the second half of his sentence escaped. A litter of little ones ran out from behind it.
We had to resort to actions. Beuys slowly spread the felt, arching it into a dark valley. I crouched and made my fingers crawl towards it like a little animal. The paper coyotes stopped and turned.
I crawled; they crawled. I went under the felt; they followed. It was crowded inside, the financial pages pressed against my face. As agreed, Beuys lifted the other end. I rolled out and he rolled up the felt. It rustled for a while like a bundle of newspapers finally willing to be quiet.
The visitors applauded. Beuys quickly turned the explanatory board to the wall.
I tiptoed towards the hat. The last paper coyote sat on its brim with the title card clenched in its mouth. I reached out. It bared a row of sharply folded letters.
I let it keep the hat.
Sources & project notes
I Like America and America Likes Me took place in New York in May 1974 with felt, newspapers, a coyote and a mesh barrier.
The time travel, fantastic events and dialogue are literary fiction; images are AI-assisted creations.

sources.title: He Fa on Albert Camus
sources.text:
1942 / France · Le Panelier, near Le Chambon-sur-Lignon
He Fa on Albert Camus
The Stamp Is Leaking Sea
I licked a stamp for Camus and nearly posted his entire lodging.
Le Panelier, 1942. The room has folded into a boat; the stamp is still leaking.
1940s black-and-white silver-gelatin fantasy stage photograph
“Don’t lick the front.”
Camus was too late. The stamp depicting the sea had already stuck to my tongue. I spat it onto the table. Seawater immediately poured from its perforated edges, sweeping away two pens, a cup and the “It’s fine” I had just uttered.
Le Panelier, late autumn 1942. I had come through the wrong backstage door only to ask directions. Now Camus stood on a chair with his manuscript raised overhead, asking whether I could swim. A little, I said. How little? A small fish jumped out of my pocket and concluded my answer.
The sea reached the tabletop. Creases appeared in the walls. All four corners folded inward, and the room creaked into the shape of a paper boat. Camus drew his foot back just in time. The window became a porthole. My shoes remained on the floor, now more properly called the hull.
He found a broom and began rowing. I hung my coat from a chair back as a sail. A gust immediately drove us towards the stamp by the table’s edge. Its pictured waves were higher than the ones outside. It was supplying our shipwreck without interruption.
“Turn it over!” Camus shouted.
I lay across the bow and reached. A wave carried the stamp away. A manuscript sheet drifted past; I tried to rescue it. Camus told me to leave it. But there was writing on it, I said. It was a shopping list, he replied. I let go, only then noticing the last item: coffee.
The hull was absorbing water. My sail worked beautifully, but took us the wrong way. I removed my other shoe to paddle while Camus pushed the bow with his broom. With two competing transport policies, we spun three times in place. On the third turn I finally reached the stamp and trapped it under the drifting cup.
For half a second the world went quiet.
The sea spiralled beneath the cup. The paper boat unfolded, the walls stood upright and the chairs returned to their places. I was still lying across the table with both wet shoes in the air. Camus counted his pages, then his pens, then looked at me.
“You can ask directions now,” he said.
I climbed down and tried to empty the cup. He stopped my hand. Seagulls cried inside it. A small mail boat was approaching a distant shore.
“Keep it for now.”
He opened the sugar tin and dropped a lump into the sea. Someone aboard the boat immediately rang a bell.
Sources & project notes
Camus arrived at Le Panelier in August 1942. The Stranger and The Myth of Sisyphus appeared that year.

sources.title: He Fa on Gilles Deleuze
sources.text:
1985 / Paris · a borrowed screening room
He Fa on Gilles Deleuze
Three Minutes on the Floor
When the projector stopped, time became a tripping hazard.
Paris, 1985. Don’t step on that frame. It has already happened once.
1985 colour-negative film with practical-effect staging
The projector clicked to a halt. Three minutes fell off the screen.
A long strip of old perforated film landed beside my shoes, little people still moving chairs inside it. Paris, 1985. I crouched to pick it up. As my finger touched a frame, the chair behind me slid back to its previous place. I stumbled and sat down backwards.
Deleuze raised a foot to let a recently elapsed cough crawl beneath his sole. Sure enough, someone coughed again.
“Don’t crumple it,” he said.
I had already squeezed several seconds into a ball. By the door the projectionist began bending down repeatedly, picking up the same screwdriver, putting it down and picking it up again. He looked at me, his anger freshly renewed each time. I hurriedly smoothed the strip. At last he could straighten up.
We needed to feed time back into the machine, but the more we pulled, the longer the strip grew. I picked up the second of my arrival. The door immediately opened; another newly arrived me almost came in. Deleuze pinned that frame with the tip of his shoe. Outside, I heard myself ask, “Is this the toilet?”
He looked at me. I said I had indeed been looking for it.
Tea began pouring backwards from a cup into the kettle. In the back row someone put on a coat in reverse, then removed it in reverse. Whenever anyone stepped on the film, the room repeated that frame. I climbed onto a chair. The chair was in the film too. It carried me sliding back towards the door.
Deleuze picked up the scissors the projectionist had left beside a chair. Thinking he meant to cut my entrance, I hastily gripped the chair back. He pointed to six quiet frames on the floor: the door stood open, nobody arriving, nobody leaving.
We joined them together. The projectionist turned the reel and an unoccupied gap appeared in the doorway. I jumped from the chair and stepped through, Deleuze following close behind. He returned the scissors to the projectionist. The door slammed, and the chairs inside finally stopped running.
Back at my theatre I discovered a short strip in my pocket: exactly one minute. I placed it beside my cold tea and slowly dragged it backwards. Steam rose from the cup. Delighted, I dragged a little further.
The tea leaves returned to their paper packet. The cup was empty.
I had to boil the kettle again.
Sources & project notes
Éditions de Minuit published the French edition of Cinema 2: The Time-Image in Paris in 1985.
The time travel, fantastic events and dialogue are literary fiction; images are AI-assisted creations.

sources.title: He Fa on David Graeber
sources.text:
2014 / London · a borrowed meeting room
He Fa on David Graeber
The Meeting Has Reached Downstairs
I added an agenda item. The whole table extended through the doorway.
London, 2014. The agenda is being eaten; the table still extends along the stairs.
2014 direct-flash digital snapshot with practical fantasy staging
Nobody noticed the first time the table grew.
London, 2014. I had borrowed a room to discuss a film. Graeber sat at the far end. I added an item on allocating equipment. With a crack, another section joined the tabletop and he slid half a metre backwards, chair and all. Steadying his cup, he asked how many items remained.
Not many, I said. Just three.
The table cracked three times and pushed the door open.
Someone proposed first discussing why this was happening. Another section immediately appeared in the corridor. I chased Graeber, who had reached the stairs. Notebooks slid along the surface. We had to conduct the meeting on foot. Each added question made the table grow farther.
Someone downstairs asked where we were going. I said we did not know; we would have to discuss it. The wood turned a corner and carried me outdoors. London wind scattered the agenda. Graeber caught a sheet and noticed that its edges had browned.
He broke off a corner and tasted it.
“Biscuit,” he said.
I said it was printer paper. He broke off another piece for me. It was indeed biscuit, slightly salty with the warmth of a printer. He ate “confirm venue.” The table immediately shortened by a section. Far away someone stumbled and finally caught up with their chair.
I promptly announced that we ought to organise a working group to eat the agenda.
The table grew again.
Graeber glared at me, pushed the remaining half-page into my hand and went to fetch the unopened bag of bread from the meeting room. We shared food along the table without discussing who was responsible for eating. Someone tore the budget in half and asked whether that was enough. I nodded. Someone picked off a visibly burnt piece labelled “follow-up work” and passed it to a willing neighbour.
At last only “any other business” remained. Nobody wanted to touch it in case more agenda items were hidden inside. Graeber rolled it into the bread and bit down. The table thundered back into the building. We ran after it with our bowls. Graeber covered his mouth as he ran, afraid of coughing out the other business.
The final section refused to return. It pushed through my theatre’s backstage door and stopped beside the sink. I put my red ticket stub on it to confirm that I was home.
Graeber’s hand reached through the doorway with the last empty bowl. I was about to ask who would wash it. He pointed at the table’s edge. I closed my mouth and turned on the tap.
Sources & project notes
Graeber joined LSE in 2013 and publicly discussed democratic practice and organisation during this period.
The time travel, fantastic events and dialogue are literary fiction; images are AI-assisted creations.

sources.title: He Fa on Leonardo da Vinci
sources.text:
1504 / Florence, workshop
He Fa on Leonardo da Vinci
The Portrait Takes the Day Off
I only glanced at an empty frame. It recruited me into the Renaissance.
“I am alive.” “So was the last one.”
Early sixteenth-century tempera and oil-on-panel vocabulary; AI fiction
The woman in the painting put one foot out first, stepped on Leonardo's palette, lifted her skirt and left. He followed her to the door. Your face is not finished, he called. By the time you finish, she said, I will not need lunch any more.
Florence, 1504. I had only just pushed through the wrong backstage door in my own theatre. Before I could ask directions, the empty frame inhaled and sucked me in. My shoulders flattened, then my stomach. My glasses refused and stuck out beyond the surface. My first successful attempt at losing weight had left me unable to turn sideways.
Leonardo returned and looked me over. This will not do. I agreed and asked him to get me out. He picked up his brush, intending to deal with my nose first.
“I am alive.” “So was the last one.”
Every stroke removed another movement I could make. My left hand was fixed, then my right. I tried shouting, but my voice came out of a small portrait next door. The unfamiliar gentleman frowned at the noise. Sorry, I said. First time using this.
Leonardo asked me to keep smiling. Having worked in theatre, I knew “a little longer” seldom had a defined limit. Until what year? I asked. He dipped his brush. Without waiting, I stretched my mouth as wide as it would go and sent my eyebrows off in opposite directions. The frame creaked. Gold leaf fell from a corner into the paint bowl.
“Do not move!” he shouted. Every portrait in the workshop froze. Even the half-painted horse in the corner stopped with a foreleg in the air. He looked from me to his own hand, apparently discovering a new application for instructions.
I reached for the red ticket stub in my pocket. Halfway out, it flattened into paint too. I stuck it over my mouth as an enormous tongue. The gentleman next door laughed. A crack opened in his frame. Laughter travelled along the wall. A saint's shoulders shook. The horse reached out of its painting and kicked over a bucket.
Leonardo did not tell us to stop again. He painted a very small door in the bottom right corner of my picture. I pulled in my stomach, folded myself twice and squeezed through. How was it? he asked. Portraits ought to have fire exits, I said.
The woman returned with her flatbread. Finding her place occupied, she looked at me, then at him. Are we still painting? Before Leonardo could answer, the empty frame on the floor had crept up to his feet.
Sources & project notes
Leonardo worked in Florence from 1500 to 1506.
The time travel, transformations and all dialogue are fiction; the image is contemporary AI-assisted work.

sources.title: He Fa on Napoleon
sources.text:
1812 / Russia, halt after the departure from Moscow
He Fa on Napoleon
Your Majesty, Flatten the Road First
Napoleon folded the map once. The road ahead stood up.
He pressed his hat down. The road slowly opened.
Early nineteenth-century hand-coloured etching vocabulary; AI fiction
Napoleon folded the map in half. The road ahead stood upright. The horses stopped, the carts stopped, and I lunged to catch the roadside before I fell out of Russia and under the table.
It was October 1812. We were leaving Moscow. I had stepped out from backstage intending to ask where the dressing room was. An officer pushed a map into my hands and told me to hold it steady. The map was light. The world inside it was heavy, and Napoleon kept adding orders.
“How much walking does one fold save?” he asked. I did not know and advised him not to try. He had already made a second fold. The distant convoy hung down from the sky, its wheels still turning diligently. A soldier's hat fell in front of us, followed by my own shout from a moment before, arriving half a beat late.
He was pleased. Much closer now, he said. I pointed at the hanging road. Closer to where? He bent to read a place name. His thumb covered a town. I asked him to move it. The town gave a sigh of relief and puffed a little smoke from its chimneys.
I tried smoothing a crease. The muddy road lowered a little. Napoleon held the opposite corner, afraid I would lose the distance he had gained. Pulling at opposite ends, we turned the road into an enormous pocket. People and carts slid towards its bottom. I let go. The pocket sprang up and left both of us hanging from the map's border.
We dangled above the blank reverse of the paper. Napoleon still tried to gesture commands. Hold on first, I said. My army is waiting, he said. So are my hands, I said, and they cannot wait much longer.
At last he gripped the border with both hands. I took out the red ticket stub to write for help, then realised I had nowhere to send a single word. We swung together like two very undignified pendulums. On the third swing, we reached the curling paper corner.
“Put something on it!” I shouted. He searched a pocket and produced a letter: too light. He touched his hat and hesitated. It is more useful than your head now, I said. He pressed it down.
The road slowly opened. Wheels met mud again. Lying flat, I pushed out the final crease, too breathless to speak. But the hat kept growing, swelling into a black mountain at the junction. An officer ran up to ask the mountain's name.
Napoleon looked towards his own bare head and said nothing. Holding the map for him, I dared not fold it again and had to walk with it above my head. In the distance, a bird landed and began building a nest on the hat mountain.
Sources & project notes
The French army departed Moscow in October 1812. The map, folding roads and hat mountain are invented.
The time travel, magic and all dialogue are fiction; the image is not evidence of the campaign.

sources.title: He Fa on Nietzsche
sources.text:
1883 / Sils Maria, Switzerland
He Fa on Nietzsche
My Footprints Have Their Own Plans
My body was still catching its breath. My footprints had already completed another circuit.
I got up quickly. Things were complicated enough already.
1880s albumen print and composite-negative vocabulary; AI fiction
The third time we passed the same rock, I put a pebble on it. The fourth time, there were two. The fifth time, the pebbles made an arrow pointing at my shoes. Do not blame the mountain yet, Nietzsche said.
Sils, summer 1883. I was walking with him, and the backstage door I had come through had disappeared. Looking down, I saw my footprints standing up out of the mud: two black soles with nobody in them, walking faster than I could.
When I chased them, they stopped. When I stopped, they walked on. Nietzsche crouched to investigate and the left footprint stepped on his hand. The right one went politely around him. I asked where they were going. They led us back to the rock. Nietzsche took out paper to write. I held his pen. Let us get home before you publish.
The footprints refused. They circled the rock, and the road behind us circled with them. The lake flipped up onto the mountain; the mountain moved beside the lake. I sat down. The impression left by my backside began to stir. I got up quickly. Things were complicated enough already.
Nietzsche told me to take off my shoes. I did. The shoes immediately chased their own footprints, apparently pleased to have lost their owner. He handed me his stick as I stood barefoot. Now what? Wait, he said. I reminded him that the soles of my feet were not writing materials.
He tried trapping them beneath his hat. With the left footprint caught, the right ran round the brim, faster and faster. He held the hat down while I caught the returning shoes. The mountain stopped moving, but the lake remained halfway up it. Several fish watched us from treetops.
I put my shoes on the wrong feet and took one step backwards. The footprints hesitated. They conferred with a sound like two books slapping together. Then one went forwards and the other backwards, tearing an opening in their own road.
“Now,” I said. We stepped through the tear and arrived outside his lodging. The mountain dropped back into place. Two fish remained on the windowsill. Nietzsche stopped and looked down. His own footprints were looking up, evidently with something to say.
I did not wait to hear it. As I hurried to open the door, the red ticket stub fell from my pocket and the unoccupied shoes stepped on it. I reached for it; they moved forward. I moved back; they did too. Nietzsche stood beside us taking notes, showing no intention of helping.
Sources & project notes
Nietzsche stayed in Sils Maria in summer 1883. The looping path and living footprints are invented.
All dialogue and fantastic events are fiction; the image is not a historical photograph.

sources.title: He Fa on Shakespeare
sources.text:
1601 / London, performance day at the Globe
He Fa on Shakespeare
Please Swallow the Ending
I read one wrong line, and the Globe began packing itself away.
The cheapest standing tickets soon acquired private-box accommodation.
Early seventeenth-century woodcut vocabulary; AI fiction
Shakespeare pushed a sheet into my hand. They were one person short; I should go on and read it. I said I did not understand. Just read what is there. That instruction had got me into plenty of performances. I had not expected it to be in use in 1601.
On the Globe's stage, I read “Bring a chair.” A chair promptly fell out of my mouth onto my foot. The audience applauded. Through the pain, I asked Shakespeare what this paper was. He drew it slightly back. Something new, he said.
Once spoken, the lines grew into solid objects. I said sword. A sword hung from my tongue. I quickly closed my mouth and broke it in two. A child near the stage collected one half. Shakespeare crouched to inspect the break and complained that I had shortened his monologue.
The actor playing the king arrived and ordered me off. I read “Exit” from the paper. The floor suddenly withdrew. The front row's toes touched the stage. The second gallery bent towards the first. The theatre squeezed inward, fold after fold, like an accordion. The cheapest standing tickets soon acquired private-box accommodation.
Shakespeare grabbed my collar and jumped a closing gap. Who told you to read the stage direction? You did not mark it, I said. It was written for someone who could read. As I began to object, a beam folded down above us. We dropped together.
The words on the sheet queued to enter my mouth, impatient to finish the evening's work. I clenched my teeth but swallowed one “door.” Knocking immediately sounded inside my stomach. Shakespeare put his ear against it. How many are in there? This is no time to sell tickets, I said.
The final “Dismiss the audience” had already risen into the air like a pair of enormous iron scissors, ready to cut the compressed theatre apart. Shakespeare caught one end; I caught the other. Whoever let go would have to swim home through the Thames.
I remembered the red ticket stub in my pocket: no returns or exchanges. I did not dare read it aloud. Lying on floorboards that now stood upright, we each bit one side of the final line and chewed the ending back into our mouths. It tasted of ink and unpaid wages.
The theatre slowly flattened. The chairs returned beneath their occupants. The child still had the sword. The king complained about the delay and called for the next scene. I shook my head and held my stomach. Someone inside knocked three times. Shakespeare had already sat down with his pen, waiting to hear who it was.
Sources & project notes
The Globe opened in 1599; penny admission to its yard is documented. No historical play is identified.
The folding theatre, solid words and all dialogue are fiction; the image is AI-assisted.

sources.title: He Fa on Van Gogh
sources.text:
1888 / The Yellow House, Arles, France
He Fa on Van Gogh
The Chair Refuses to Wait
Gauguin had not arrived. The chair prepared for him left first.
“Rescue first, draw later!”
1880s reed-pen and watercolour vocabulary; AI fiction
As soon as Van Gogh finished its fourth leg, the chair climbed off the paper, knocked over the ink bottle and ran. We chased it to the Yellow House doorway. In the middle of the street it paused, shook paint from its wooden legs and accelerated.
Arles, October 1888. Gauguin had not arrived, and the chair had evidently lost patience. Van Gogh pursued it with his pen. Wait, I said. You have not told me what it eats. Chairs do not eat. Then why is it heading for the restaurant?
The real chair by the door saw it and followed. Then the upstairs chairs, the neighbours' chairs, the chairs outside the restaurant. Wood began striking stone all along the street. Several people still sitting were carried away before they could get up, soup bowls in their hands.
I caught the painted chair from behind. It immediately stopped, apparently pleased to have found a passenger. As I relaxed, it flung me into its seat and ran on. Van Gogh kept pace beside me. I reached for his help, but he was studying the moving legs and muttering something.
“Rescue first, draw later!” I shouted. He put his pen behind his ear and caught the chair back. The chair dragged us round a corner, its rear legs crossing a gutter while the others crushed his shoes. Looking down, I saw familiar yellow paint spreading over the seat and staining my trousers into part of it.
It wanted to keep me. I tried to stand, but beneath my backside came the sound of wet paint pulling apart. Do not force it, Van Gogh said. Should I wait for it to dry? Ahead, a restaurant table stood up and blocked the door, apparently opposing this unauthorised expansion of the chair business.
Van Gogh crouched and drew a very long table on a sheet. Before adding legs, he asked me to hold it. I pulled the red ticket stub free of the chair and clipped down a corner of the sheet. He quickly added four stout legs and pushed the paper into the street.
The long table sprang up with a thump, blocking the whole road. The chairs braked and crowded round it, finding their places one after another. Mine joined them and finally released my trousers. Someone put their remaining soup on the table. Bread followed from the roadside. Van Gogh sat opposite me, his sleeves covered in ink.
What now? I asked. He was already drawing a bowl. I held down the sheet and suggested that the bowl should have something in it first. He changed two strokes. A freshly drawn fish leapt out, flicked its tail and knocked the red ticket into the soup.
Sources & project notes
Letters document Van Gogh furnishing the Yellow House and awaiting Gauguin in October 1888.
The living furniture, He Fa’s visit and all dialogue are fiction; the image is not an original Van Gogh.

sources.title: He Fa on Andy Warhol
sources.text:
1964 / New York · the Silver Factory
He Fa on Andy Warhol
The One in the Camera Won’t Clock Off
I came for a screen test. The He Fa on screen got the job first.
New York, 1964. The other He Fa takes the chair first.
1964 black-and-white documentary and optical double-exposure character
As soon as the camera started, the me on screen stood up.
I remained seated.
The Silver Factory, New York, 1964. Warhol had asked me to move as little as possible. The He Fa on screen plainly had not received the instruction. He straightened his shirt and gestured for me to get up. I tried to raise my hand; it grew heavier. He grew nimbler, stepping over the screen’s lower edge into the room, a strip of white light trailing from his sole.
“Sit back down,” I said.
He brushed my words aside and took my chair. The screen scooped me up like a bedsheet. I clung to its frame as my body grew thinner and my nose disappeared in profile. Only then did I remember that the film recorded no sound. I opened my mouth to shout. The machine was the only thing heard in the room.
Warhol came closer to inspect, then stepped back to adjust the shot.
The double pointed at me as though requesting the replacement of an inadequate prop. I pushed an arm out of the screen and grabbed the chair back, hoping to pull him in. He casually hung his coat on my hand. This He Fa was already better suited to New York.
I felt in my pocket. Everything had flattened except the stiff red ticket stub. While Warhol looked aside, I covered the lens with it. Something clicked, and every exchange stopped. I had one leg inside the screen and one outside. The double froze halfway through crossing his legs.
“We’re missing a section,” Warhol said.
On the back of the stub I wrote: Let me out first.
He took the paper, read it and nodded. I uncovered a sliver of lens. The double immediately moved. I covered it again; his smile froze across half his face. After three attempts, we reached an agreement: he would sit for me by day, I would come out at night, and each could use half the name.
Warhol labelled the film can “HE / FA.” The double objected to the order of the credits. I reminded him that he had not spoken a single word. Warhol pointed at the camera, indicating that neither had I.
At changeover I finally squeezed out of the screen, flexing my nose first and then my shoulders. The double settled inside, already better than me at checking his watch impatiently. I was about to leave when a second camera started at the other end of the room.
The He Fa on screen and I turned round together.
Sources & project notes
Warhol made the Screen Tests in 1964–66 as silent 16mm film portraits, usually projected in slow motion.
The time travel, fantastic events and dialogue are literary fiction; images are AI-assisted creations.

sources.text:
How Works Happen · Archival Research
How Works Happen: Theatre, Assessment and Agreements for Working Together
Eight encounters with P4 and US-period materials: who acts, how media take part, and how an action becomes a work.
Archival research and editorial compilation · 2 October 2026 · AI-assisted interpretation and English translation, not an artist’s statement.
Begin with a scene
In these materials, P4 is both a theatre space for working together and a platform offering space, documentation, organisation and planning. The public Personal Chronicle proposal brings watching, performing and filming together. To understand this practice, we need to see how people use a space, initiate actions and leave records, rather than simply list productions.
The lights go down, but singing comes from outside the stage. A performer in white descends from the upper floor; only later does the audience see a second performer, dressed in black, behind the gauze. Projections, bodies, written words, music and broadcasts keep redirecting attention. This opening is described in a retained Shadow Counterpoint press text. That account also records a difficulty: some spectators felt that the juxtaposition divided their attention and that the words did not clarify the story.

Start with space and shared practice, then compare the three questions below.
Sources and scope:
S03
·
S12
Three questions to carry through the materials
How do existing images, texts and bodily experience become actions that several people can carry out together? Who decides what an action means: makers, participants, a machine or assessors? When does an action begin and end, and how does its record let others enter it? These questions take concrete form in gauze and projections, translation interfaces, assessment documents, paper scripts and public project agreements. They are ways to compare particular materials, rather than a single theme imposed on every work.

Sources and scope:
S03
·
S04
·
S05
·
S10

S12
Four windows in time
The first concerns early theatre collaboration. The 2016 Shadow Counterpoint texts describe a practical spatial problem: how existing images and music coexist with performance, and how spectators divide their attention. Two press texts credit He Fa and Aoshuang with planning and Yan Qin with direction. Preservation in He Fa’s archive does not make every contribution his.
The second concerns documented US-period work. A Fa’s review work list dated 28 April 2017 identifies the assessment itself as documentary work. Some Fafalish Library photographs carry a device date of 24 October 2017 and show paper, letterforms, computer operations and onlookers. They can be compared through questions of judgement and reading, but the materials do not establish that the assessment caused the later experiments.
The third concerns shared exercises around 2021–2022. Lisa workshop photographs show both two people standing face to face and exchanges around paper and materials. In Feedback, reading and physical actions alternate; in Outward Monologue, thread and a curtain alter what can be seen between bodies. Camera dates support the workshop records; directory labels supply the other two dates. These are different kinds of evidence, not a precise chronology.
The fourth is a public organisational proposal from 2023. The Personal Chronicle recruitment text connects an interview, project initiation, process documentation and a public presentation. Publication establishes that the procedure was proposed, not that every project completed it.
The US period is a parallel strand in He Fa’s practice, not an American phase of P4 as a whole. These windows organise a reading, not a complete institutional history.

These windows do not mean that He Fa first resolved images, then moved to bodies and finally to organisation. Images were already part of theatre, and US-period proposals also addressed shared work. Long Long Ago Group proposed that participants take turns hosting activities in their own regions while continuing to attend one another’s activities, and jointly seek alternatives when a venue was unsuitable. Eight encounters, organised by questions
Begin with the Shadow Counterpoint reports to understand the practical difficulty of coordinating media. Then read the Fa’s review assessment and work list to see how an evaluation becomes part of a work. Fafalish Library photographs bring paper, screens and onlookers around the same table; the Lisa workshop moves between facing another person and gathering around materials.
Outward Monologue and Feedback show different bodily processes: thread and concealment in one, paper and repeated movements in the other. Out of Everyday Life places paper within a seated exchange, though its contents and any decisions remain unknown. Finally, the publication of Personal Chronicle sets out proposed beginnings and endings for projects. The first seven encounters have varying degrees of visual or documentary support; the eighth is first of all the publication of a proposal, not proof of subsequent delivery.

· He Fa
Chapter 2 · The Person Who Says “I Love You”
A Sentence Changes Its Use
At the beginning of
Shoot Self with You
, Jia Rui says, ‘I love you.’ A little later, Zi Chou says, ‘The acting is terrible.’
[2-1]
¶
Between the two sentences, the listener shifts from one role to another. The first offers a declaration of love; the second looks back to assess that expression. Someone who was just reaching toward another person has become a performer being watched. He has finished speaking, yet what his words amount to has become a question again.
¶
Watch the passage: How a Declaration of Love Becomes a Judgment of Acting
Video · bilingual dialogue · stills · return to this paragraph
I do not want to find proof of a feeling hidden beneath the lines of this declaration. Discovering the actors’ private feelings would not make the scene easier to understand. What deserves attention is that two demands fall on the same person at once: he needs to speak to his partner, and he needs to make his speaking worth watching. The other person can receive what he expresses, or step outside it and judge his performance. Acting thus carries an asymmetry: I am still speaking to you, while you are already watching how I speak.
¶
This shift also means that what is ‘real’ in a film cannot be measured by intensity of commitment alone. If an actor cries, the tears really occur; what they express still depends on the action in which they appear. Someone who does not cry may also render a difficult grief precisely. Feelings and the ability to express them do not always arrive at the same moment. Demanding that they coincide completely can keep actors so busy proving what is inside them that they have no time to hear the person beside them.
¶
‘The acting is terrible’ can, of course, be a useful judgment. Without judgments about expression, rehearsal would struggle to continue. But a judgment needs to contain something that can be answered: what was unclear just now, which action came too soon, or who had not yet been given time to respond. If evaluation stays at the level of real or fake, performers can only keep offering themselves up, waiting for someone else to announce that this time they are finally real enough.
¶
I want the film to keep this shift visible. It allows viewers to see how intimate words become work, and how judgments about that work enter the process of people drawing closer. Declarations of love and evaluations each have their uses. When they meet, they can also interrupt one another.
¶
Shoot Self with You, still from the fixed 4K master. At the opening, three people occupy different distances within one frame.
Shoot Self with You, collectively created by the cast and crew; still from the fixed master.
A Role Gives Someone a Position
A role allows someone to do something with others without first having to explain themselves in full. They can say a line that has already been written, carry out an agreed action, or begin by knowing whom to turn toward. Something difficult to say in ordinary life can sometimes take shape through this distance. Fiction gives action a starting point, and leaves the person a little room to retreat: this sentence is happening within the play, so I can try saying it.
¶
In an article written before the performance, Sun Jiarui describes how acting allowed him to meet people and become their friend, and how it became a way of feeling needed. He also writes about his dislike of himself in photographs, his surprise after agreeing to perform, and his intention to stop acting.
[2-2]
These parts should be read together. A role gives him a way in, but may also narrow that entrance. Others need this actor, and so he can remain part of their shared life. How else might he be needed once he leaves the actor’s position? That becomes a harder question to answer.
¶
What I see here is a dependence that enthusiasm can easily conceal in creative work. Doing things together produces relations, but those relations may then require a person to keep serving a particular purpose. Someone who is always ready with a reply is expected to keep replying. Someone willing to take on a difficult role is invited to do so again. The ability that first gave them entry gradually becomes the main way others recognize them. The more successful the role, the easier it is for the particular person to be hidden behind it.
¶
This does not mean collaboration should have no division of tasks. It is precisely through different abilities that people can work together. The problem is when a person’s assigned part comes to be understood as all that they are. If someone refuses to perform next time, do they lose a work arrangement, or also their place among the others? ‘We’re all friends’ cannot answer that question in advance. It depends on how people continue to see one another after someone stops serving a function.
¶
I therefore want to think of a role as a place one can enter and also leave. It should allow tentative attempts: speaking with someone else’s sentences and discovering one’s own voice; completing a task and discovering that one no longer wants to do it this way. The relations a role opens up deserve to be tested beyond that role.
¶
Knowing It Is Acting, Still Wanting to Argue Back
After the performance, Sun Jiarui wrote: ‘I know
He Fa
is acting, but I really do want to argue back.’
[2-3]
¶
This sentence makes the effect of performance precise. He recognizes it as acting, yet the wish to argue back still arises. Knowing that something belongs to a play does not exempt him from its effects. An actor can know perfectly well that the other person is speaking lines and still be angered or moved by what they say, or feel that an arrangement ought to change. Fiction has real effects precisely because the people taking part in it have not left reality: they are still spending time, waiting for one another, judging the action before them, and carrying it out with their own bodies.
¶
Yet we cannot gather all these effects under the phrase ‘getting into character.’ Getting into character is often understood as forgetting oneself, as if actors can only feel something real by temporarily losing the ability to distinguish what is happening. Jia Rui’s words retain that distinction. He knows he is performing, and he has his own judgment. The urge to argue back coexists with his awareness of the play. A person can participate in a framework while also judging it from within.
¶
This is part of what makes fiction interesting. It lets someone borrow another situation while retaining some distance from it. A person can try actions they would not ordinarily take and discover their limits in the attempt. Complete immersion is only one state of performance. Remaining aware, hesitating, or occasionally stepping out of a role can also produce powerful expression. A film can bring these different states together, allowing a character’s actions and an actor’s judgments to illuminate one another.
¶
Someone may ask: if real relations matter, why not simply talk directly? Because ‘directly’ has conditions of its own. The names we call one another, our habits, and our expectations in ordinary life already determine much of who can say what and how far they can go. Taking on another role can sometimes move those arrangements a little. People do not always have a complete self first and then search for the right sentences to convey it. Sometimes only after speaking and acting do they discover that this is how they respond.
¶
I value this discovery, but do not want to possess it. A maker can arrange a task that allows a sentence to be spoken. What that sentence later means to the speaker is something the speaker must go on understanding. The work preserves the expression, while the person’s interpretation continues to change.
¶
No Single Kind of Truth Can Answer Everything
At this point, several things that easily become entangled need to be separated. Whether a line was actually spoken is something a recording can help establish. To understand what someone felt while speaking, we need to hear their account. Whether that expression changed how people related to one another requires looking at what they did next. Whether the film gave these changes a forceful organization takes us back to its sounds, images, and rhythms.
¶
All four questions matter. When they are mixed together, a work can acquire a value from the weight of lived experience that seems to need no further explanation: someone was really distressed, so this passage must remain; the collaboration was unforgettable, so viewers ought to be moved. But viewers did not share those days. They are facing a film and need to establish a relation to it through what it gives them. A pause familiar to its makers may still be a blank for a stranger. Turning that blank into a waiting the viewer can feel is work the film’s form has to do.
¶
Conversely, a moving film does not prescribe how the people involved should remember what happened. Artistic success cannot account for every value of an encounter. Someone may cherish the film while remaining unhappy with a particular arrangement. Someone else may have no interest in the finished film yet cherish an afternoon of working together. These differences should be allowed to remain around the work.
¶
My position is therefore clear: art can actively create the conditions under which people meet. It need not wait for an entirely authentic life to appear of its own accord. Roles, sets, lines, and cameras can all give experience ways of being expressed that it did not have before. Art’s strength also comes from a limit: participants can always bring something that the arrangement has not yet included.
¶
When someone says ‘I love you,’ they borrow a sentence countless people have spoken, yet still address it, at this moment, to a particular person. The listener may answer, hesitate, or judge the performance. Where the next sentence takes this relation cannot be determined by the first sentence alone. The film’s work begins here: to preserve how a reply is awaited, missed, or changed.
¶

· He Fa
Chapter 3 · Once More
The Last Attempt Remains in the Body
“Once more” is one of the most ordinary things said in rehearsal, and perhaps one of the hardest requests to understand. What are we repeating? A sequence of movements, a line, a feeling that has already gone, or an approach that failed to begin just now? The person saying it may think the meaning is clear, but the person doing it has to decide what to carry into the next attempt.
¶
This suggestion also appears in
Shoot Self with You
.
[3-1]
I want to pause first over the word “again.” It points to the past but calls for a future action. The next attempt will not begin from nothing: the participants have already heard feedback, know that a particular action has failed, and may have become more familiar with their partners, or may already be tired. Repetition always carries something left by the previous attempt. Even when the lines and positions are exactly the same, what people have to deal with may have changed.
¶
Watch the passage: What Does “One More Time” Ask Us to Repeat?
Video · bilingual dialogue · stills · return to this paragraph
Starting again can therefore both correct and accumulate. A sequence that initially required thought can later be completed smoothly; an answer that could be tried at first may no longer appear because it has already been rejected. Repetition brings proficiency, and it also brings expectations. People gradually learn what will be accepted. That knowledge can help them work together, but it can also make them deliver the right answer before the other person has finished speaking.
¶
I do not place contingency in opposition to proficiency. If a partner unexpectedly changes speed, someone practised may have more room to respond; someone entirely unprepared may only be able to fall back on the actions they first memorized. What matters is what capacities practice has freed up, and what attention it has taken over. Once an action can be performed reliably, can the person still hear the difference between this attempt and the last?
¶
Sameness then has two uses. It can let people retreat into a result they already know, or provide a stable place from which small changes can finally be noticed. If everything changes on every attempt, change becomes harder to distinguish. Keeping some things in place makes it possible to see how others move. Freedom in creative work sometimes needs such fixed points.
¶
A rehearsal for Kill That Rose. First published in a performance countdown article on 11 June 2021.
P4 Theater archive; no separately verified photographer credit was found for this image.
What Counts as Finished?
A request that can be carried out can usually also specify when it has been fulfilled. Wait for the other person to finish before beginning your own line; walk to a particular place and pause; make a word audible to the back row. The actor can try, the director can explain, and the next attempt can be compared with the last. They may not agree quickly, but their disagreement has an object they can work on together.
¶
“Make it more real” may move that object out of reach. The actor has completed the action but must also prove that they are present in it; if they explain that they feel something, they may then be judged too deliberate. The more authenticity is demanded, the more the actor needs to watch how they appear. They try to enter the scene while checking from the outside whether they have entered it. A command to be natural can make people work ever harder to manage their naturalness.
¶
Gentleness and severity cannot distinguish good rehearsal here. A precise request can be demanding and frustrating, while broad encouragement may never give anyone something they can actually do. The artist should take on the difficulty of turning judgment into work. If an attempt lacks force, where exactly does it fall short? Are the actions unrelated, the words addressed to no one, or does the rhythm leave no time for a response? A feeling may not be immediately nameable, but the work should still begin with something that can be tried.
¶
I am especially wary of treating commitment as an unlimited resource. What an actor has already expressed may be judged not good enough, but that judgment cannot simply become a judgment of the whole person. It is this attempt that has failed; the person’s entire authenticity should not therefore be put on trial. Rehearsal needs to make room for an attempt that has not gone well, so that the next can be work rather than another act of self-defence.
¶
The strongest objection to this position is that art takes people precisely where no method yet exists. If every request is completely clear, would all that remains be execution? I agree that the unknown cannot be eliminated. A director may not be able to say in advance what they are looking for, but they can work with the actors to identify the differences that emerge in each attempt, and acknowledge that they have not yet found it this time. The question is who bears the unknown. An artist cannot preserve the ambiguity of their own judgment while demanding definite proof of the participants’ inner lives.
¶
Finishing does not always mean reaching an ideal result. Sometimes it means having seen clearly that continuing with this method will bring us no closer to what we are looking for. Only when we can end one method can we begin another.
¶
Letting the Lines Step Back a Little
In a 2018 interview, Ryusuke Hamaguchi discussed repeated script readings: first, without imposing a fixed tone, the actors read until they have thoroughly absorbed the words; then, during filming, they let their expression respond to the moment and their partners.
[3-2]
What interests me is the arrangement between these two stages. Repetition takes on part of the work of remembering, so that when filming begins, the actors do not have to devote all their attention to “What is my next line?”
¶
This suggests a limited claim: preparation can change how attention is distributed. When the lines are relatively secure, an actor may notice a partner’s hesitation and adjust the timing of their own entry. The text has not disappeared, but it has receded a little. The person has a chance to respond to what is happening. Listening here includes sound, but also waiting: allowing the other person’s expression on this attempt to arrive a little later, more quietly, or with a pause absent from the last.
¶
This arrangement can also lead to the opposite result. Once actors have memorized the text, they may be even more eager to complete the sequence they already know; what is called natural is merely the precise reproduction of a practised manner. A method’s name does not determine its effect. What needs to be observed is whether, after repetition, actors have more ways to respond to change, or are left only with smoother execution.
¶
There is an actual timeline connecting
P4
and Hamaguchi. In a 2023 article, Yun Jianhui recalled that we had already discussed Hamaguchi’s work in 2022; after
Shoot Self with You
began, the early crew studied
Intimacies
, and lines from that film entered the script in July of the same year.
[3-3]
This record shows that the film had become part of our shared work. For me, the question more worth pursuing is how those studies changed the way we worked. There is still a long way between liking a film and making its method work among another group of people.
¶
What I take from repeated script reading does not require every creative work to follow the same procedure. It draws my attention to a question that enthusiasm often obscures: how many things can a person handle at once while expressing themselves? Remembering lines, searching for emotion, attending to the camera, and guessing how pleased the director is can easily fill all one’s attention with one’s own tasks. Entrusting some of this to practice is meant to free up the capacity to attend to other people.
¶
Listening in art therefore needs to be arranged. It can begin by reducing certain tasks, fixing a standing position, or making a sentence clear. Asking someone to open up their whole self is often too much; enabling them to hear the sentence in front of them through to its end is sometimes already difficult.
¶
The Kill That Rose team, 2021. People sit together around a computer, papers and cups.
P4 Theater archive; no separately verified photographer credit was found for this image.
Allowing an Attempt to Have No Shape Yet
Another value of repetition is that it allows awkwardness to remain in the work for a while. When an action is new, the body often moves more slowly than the intention. Knowing that one wants to come closer does not mean already knowing how to stand, where to put one’s hands, or how to leave the other person enough support. If a complete action is demanded too soon, participants can easily choose a familiar performance posture that makes the difficulty disappear from the image.
¶
The difficulty may be covered over without the action having been resolved. A familiar way of performing intimacy may conceal how two people actually approach each other; an uneven attempt may instead reveal what needs adjusting. I am willing to give such attempts time. But awkwardness does not thereby acquire an inherent aesthetic value. A pause may contain a search, or it may simply reflect a lack of preparation. Creative work needs to discern whether, after the pause, the relation between the person and the action has changed.
¶
We can imagine a simple comparison: two people repeatedly practise taking the hand the other extends. One way of practising requires the action to match the demonstration every time; another first fixes where the extended hand starts, and lets the person receiving it adjust to its actual speed. The first can train precision, the second responsiveness. Both may be useful, and they may alternate within the same rehearsal. The distinction is concrete enough that proficiency and freedom need not be set against each other.
¶
This also changes how I think about “failed footage.” Whether an attempt is worth including in a film depends on what it changes. If viewers can see how two people adjust and begin to wait for one another, slowness has content of its own. If only embarrassment is shown repeatedly, while the participants gain no new action, extending the viewing may merely increase their exposure. Keeping failure requires a formal reason, just as keeping success does.
¶
Once more cannot cancel the previous attempt. What it can do is bring that attempt into a new action: I did not hear you out just now, so now I wait; I was eager to finish, and now I see that my partner is not ready; I thought it was a question of emotion, and now I hear the other person say it is a little hot. A small condition emerges, and what the next attempt needs to do changes with it.
¶

, 24 August 2023. The timeline is his retrospective account from that period; it does not establish that
P4
adopted Hamaguchi’s rehearsal procedure in full.
